L29: Classification of hyperspectral remote sensing images is affected by two main problems: high dimensionality of the acquired signatures and scarce availability of labeled samples. Learning a low dimensional manifold and active learning represent two approaches that have been investigated in the literature to mitigate these effects. However they are usually applied independently from each other. In this paper we propose a method in which feature extraction and active learning are combined.
L30: In particular, a new reduced feature space is learned by large margin nearest neighbor (LMNN), a metric learning strategy that takes advantage of labeled information. The method is applied in conjunction with k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) classification, for which a new sample selection strategy is proposed. Experiments on a real hyperspectral dataset confirm the effectiveness of the proposed method.

L59: ABSTRACT
L60: 
L61: Classification of hyperspectral remote sensing images is
L62: 
L63: affected by two main problems: high dimensionality of the
L64: 
L65: acquired signatures and scarce availability of labeled
L66: 
L67: samples. Learning a low dimensional manifold and active
L68: 
L69: learning represent two approaches that have been
L70: 
L71: investigated in the literature to mitigate these effects.
L72: However they are usually applied independently from each
L73: 
L74: other. In this paper we propose a method in which feature
L75: 
L76: extraction and active learning are combined. In particular, a
L77: 
L78: new reduced feature space is learned by large margin nearest
L79: 
L80: neighbor (LMNN), a metric learning strategy that takes
L81: 
L82: advantage of labeled information. The method is applied in
L83: 
L84: conjunction with k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) classification,
L85: 
L86: for which a new sample selection strategy is proposed.
L87: Experiments on a real hyperspectral dataset confirm the
L88: 
L89: effectiveness of the proposed method.
L90: 
L91: Index Terms—Active learning, classification,
L92: 
L93: hyperspectral images, metric learning.
L94: 
L95: 1. INTRODUCTION
L96: 
L97: In the last few years classification of hyperspectral images
L98: 
L99: has gained great interest in the remote sensing community
L100: 
L101: thanks to the availability of se nsors with increasing spatial
L102: 
L103: and spectral resolution. This poses new methodological
L104: 
L105: challenges in image analysis due to the peculiarities that
L106: characterize this type of data.
L107: 
L108: A first relevant problem is given by the high
L109: 
L110: dimensionality of the acquired spectral signatures, which
L111: 
L112: makes standard methods used for multispectral images
L113: 
L114: suboptimal when applied to hyperspectral data. Feature
L115: 
L116: extraction is widely used to ad dress this issue, and manifold
L117: 
L118: learning is an effective extraction approach for classification
L119: 
L120: of hyperspectral data [1]–[3]. The data manifold can be
L121: 
L122: recovered within a graph embedding framework [4], where
L123: pair-wise data similarity is us ed to estimate the underlying
L124: 
L125: structure. However, this process of data manifold developing
L126: 
L127: is generally unsupervised. Inclusion of labeled information
L128: 
L129: can provide improved classification in the manifold space
L130: 
L131: [2].
L132: 
L133: Another critical problem in practical situations is
L134: 
L135: represented by the scarcity of labeled samples. Active
L136: 
L137: learning (AL) methods have been investigated recently in the
L138: 
L139: literature to increase the size of the training set and to
L140: simultaneously minimize the human user’s effort in terms of
L141: 
L142: sample labeling [5], [6]. We note how the AL process is
L143: 
L144: usually applied to the origin al features or on a reduced
L145: 
L146: feature space obtained by applying feature extraction as a
L147: 
L148: pre-processing step. However, this situation, represented in
L149: 
L150: Fig. 1(a), is suboptimal since the two steps are independent
L151: 
L152: from each other. In particular, the manifold learning
L153: 
L154: algorithm is applied on the unlabeled data with possible
L155: unsatisfactory results in terms of class separability.
L156: 
L157: 2. PROPOSED METHOD
L158: 
L159: In this paper we propose a strategy for hyperspectral image
L160: 
L161: classification in which the two steps of feature extraction
L162: 
L163: and AL are combined as depicted in Fig. 1(b). In particular
L164: 
L165: the reduced feature space is learned by LMNN [7], a metric
L166: 
L167: learning strategy that takes advantage of labeled
L168: 
L169: information. The method is applied in conjunction with k-
L170: 
L171: NN classification, for which we propose a new sample
L172: selection strategy. Although metric learning has exhibited
L173: 
L174: promising capabilities, it has been investigated in the remote
L175: 
L176: sensing literature only recently [8], [9] and not in connection
L177: 
L178: with the AL problem.
L179:

L183: 
L184: better distance measure d(x i,x j) between two generic samples
L185: 
L186: x i and x j. The Mahalanobis distance, the most common
L187: 
L188: prevailing measure, consists of finding a transformation
L189: matrix M such that

L388: 2.2 Active sampling strategy
L389: At this point, an AL strategy can be applied to the reduced
L390: 
L391: feature space to enrich the tr aining set. However, traditional
L392: 
L393: selection cannot be considered due to the peculiarities of k-
L394: 
L395: NN classifier. We propose a simple but effective strategy
L396: 
L397: inspired by the ensemble classi fier concept. For a generic
L398: 
L399: unlabeled sample, different outcomes can be obtained by
L400: 
L401: selecting different parameter k in a range [1, Q] for finding
L402: 
L403: the neighborhood. The samples that exhibit the minimum
L404: number of votes for the modal value are selected. We note
L405: 
L406: this step can be performed by only searching for Q nearest
L407: 
L408: neighbors, instead of multiple execution of searching for k
L409: 
L410: nearest neighbors for k [1, Q]. Computing the selection
L411: 
L412: criterion consists in finding the Q nearest neighbors to the
L413: 
L414: sample, and the different estimates in function of the value k
L415: 
L416: can be easily extracted since the identified nearest neighbors
L417: 
L418: automatically encode ranking information.

L420: 3. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
L421: 
L422: 3.1 Dataset
L423: The proposed active-metric learning method was evaluated
L424: 
L425: experimentally on the widely used hyperspectral Kennedy
L426: 
L427: Space Center (KSC) dataset. D ata were acquired by the
L428: 
L429: NASA Airborne Visible/Infrared Imaging Spectrometer
L430: 
L431: (AVIRIS) sensor over the KSC in March 1996, with an 18-
L432: 
L433: m spatial resolution and a 10-nm spectral resolution over the
L434: 
L435: range of 400-2500 nm. Removal of noisy and water
L436: 
L437: absorption bands resulted in 176 bands. Ground truth was
L438: 
L439: composed by 5211 labeled samples subdivided into 13
L440: classes: Scrub (761), Willow swamp (243), Cabbage hamm
L441: 
L442: (256), Cabbage palm (252), Slash pine (161), Oak (229),
L443: 
L444: Hardwood swamp (105), Graminoid marsh (431), Spartina
L445: 
L446: marsh (520), Cattail marsh (404), Salt marsh (419), Mud
L447: 
L448: flats (503), Water (927).
L449: 
L450: 3.2 Experimental setting
L451: 
L452: The objective of the experimental analysis was to compare
L453: 
L454: the proposed method with other strategies that do not
L455: 
L456: combine active and metric learning into a unique framework.
L457: 
L458: The proposed method was ap plied in conjunction with k-NN
L459: classifier (setting k=1 and thus denoted as “1NN lmnn”) and
L460: 
L461: fixing the parameter K (into LMNN) to 3. For the active
L462: 
L463: sampling strategy, k was selected as 1, 3 and 5. In terms of
L464: 
L465: comparison, three strategies that apply feature extraction
L466:

L468: 
L469: unsupervised linear PCA (1NN pca); 2) unsupervised non-
L470:

L62: ABSTRACT
L63: 
L64: Mapping of remote sensing data is usually done through im-
L65: 
L66: age classiﬁcation. For hyperspectral images, the classiﬁcation
L67: 
L68: process often relies only on the spectral signature of each sin-
L69: 
L70: gle pixel. Nevertheless, combining spatial and spectral fea-
L71: tures has been a promising way for accuracy improvement.
L72: 
L73: We address here this problem by computing spectral features
L74: 
L75: from spatially identiﬁed regions, sampled from a hierarchical
L76: 
L77: image representation, namely α-tree, built with prior knowl-
L78: 
L79: edge. The sampling of the tree nodes (i.e., regions) is based
L80: 
L81: on the paradigm of constrained connectivity and the global
L82: 
L83: range criterion. In this paper, we extend this criterion to hy-
L84: 
L85: perspectral data and apply it to our knowledge-based α-tree.
L86: Our results show an improvement of pixelwise classiﬁcation
L87: 
L88: accuracy over spectral features only.
L89: 
L90: Index Terms—Hyperspectral Image, Metric Learning,
L91: 
L92: Constrained Connectivity, Hierarchical Representation, α-
L93: 
L94: Tree, (α, ω)-Connected Components.
L95: 
L96: 1. INTRODUCTION
L97: 
L98: Thanks to the continuous growth of high and very high spatial
L99: 
L100: resolution sensors, remote sensing images contain great de-
L101: 
L102: tails that can be exploited successfully in various tasks such as
L103: object extraction or classiﬁcation. At the same time, standard
L104: 
L105: pixel-based methods for image understanding are not adapted
L106: 
L107: anymore as they can not deal with the amount of information
L108: 
L109: and with the heterogeneity of the scene. It is then manda-
L110: 
L111: tory to rely on image representation of higher level, for in-
L112: 
L113: stance through regions produced by a segmentation process.
L114: 
L115: To face the challenging issue of building a relevant segmen-
L116: 
L117: tation from satellite imagery, different multiscale representa-
L118: tions have been proposed in the literature and we focus here
L119: 
L120: on the α-tree model [1], inspired by the well-known principle
L121: 
L122: of single linkage in pattern recognition.
L123: 
L124: In a previous work [2], we have explored how to build
L125: 
L126: this model from hyperspectral data, and shown the beneﬁt of
L127: 
L128: using metric learning to measure local dissimilarity between
L129: 
L130: neighboring pixels. Nevertheless, the α-tree is limited by the
L131: 
L132: chaining effect (as any single linkage procedure). Constrained
L133: connectivity has been proposed to solve this issue [3], leading
L134: 
L135: to the deﬁnition of (α, ω)-connected components. However,
L136: 
L137: the existing computation schemes are not able to deal with
L138: 
L139: high dimension spaces such as hyperspectral images. In this
L140: 
L141: article, we ﬁrst address this issue and introduce a method for
L142: 
L143: extracting (α, ω)-connected components from an hyperspec-
L144: 
L145: tral image through its α-tree. We then extract spatial-spectral
L146: 
L147: features by sampling the hierarchical representation at differ-
L148: ent (α, ω)values, which allows to model the spatial context
L149: 
L150: of each pixel. These extracted features are then the inputs of a
L151: 
L152: SVM classiﬁer [4]. We illustrate the interest of our approach
L153: 
L154: by some improvement in pixelwise classiﬁcation.
L155: 
L156: This paper is organized as follows. We recall in Sec. 2 the
L157: 
L158: concept of α-tree, and in particular its extension to hyperspec-
L159: 
L160: tral images using metric learning. Sec. 3 deals speciﬁcally
L161: 
L162: with the drawback of the chaining effect, that is solved with
L163: constrained connectivity through a global range constraint.
L164: 
L165: We propose an efﬁcient approximation of this measure for
L166: 
L167: hyperspectral images. The interest of the proposed method is
L168: 
L169: illustrated through experimental results in Sec. 4 before con-
L170: 
L171: cluding and suggesting directions for future work.
L172: 
L173: 2. KNOWLEDGE-BASED α-TREES
L174: 
L175: 2.1. α-trees
L176: 
L177: An α-tree is a multiscale representation of an image through
L178: 
L179: its α-connected components (or α-CCs). While it ﬁnds roots
L180: in early work in computer vision, it has been revisited only
L181: 
L182: recently by Soille and Ouzounis [5, 1]. This paradigm is very
L183: 
L184: related to the single linkage procedure used in data clustering.
L185: 
L186: The concept of α-CC is an extension of the connected
L187: 
L188: component (or CC). We recall that the latter is deﬁned as a set
L189: 
L190: of adjacent pixels that share the same value (either scalar for
L191: 
L192: panchromatic images, or vectorial for multi- or hyperspectral
L193: 
L194: ones). Representing an image by its CCs allows for higher-
L195: level analysis (similarly to computer vision techniques rely-
L196: 
L197: ing on superpixels). However, the possibly great number of
L198: 
L199: CCs in an image prevents their practical use. Indeed, adjacent
L200: 
L201: pixels may belong to the same structure but have slightly dif-
L202: 
L203: ferent values, thus belonging to different CCs. The concept
L204: 
L205: of α-CC has been introduced to allow such slight variations,
L206: 
L207: leading to the following deﬁnition: an α-CC is a set of adja-
L208: 
L209: cent pixels that share similar values i.e., values with a differ-
L210: ence lower or equal to a threshold α. The α-CC of a pixel p
L211: 
L212: will thus contain all pixels q that can be reached with a path
L213: 
L214: over neighboring pixels p i h p 1=p, . . . , p n=q i from p to q
L215: 
L216: such as d(p i, p i+1)≤α.
L217: 
L218: The complexity and number of α-CCs are directly related
L219: 
L220: to α. It allows one to build a hierarchical representation of an
L221: 
L222: image, and to perform subsequent multiscale analysis (e.g., in
L223: 
L224: an object-oriented strategy). This representation is called an
L225: α-tree. Each level of the tree is indexed by an α value, and
L226: 
L227: its nodes are the corresponding α-CCs. A leaf in the tree is a
L228: 
L229: 0-CC i.e., a standard CC in the image. Increasing α leads to
L230: 
L231: the connection of α-CCs, resulting in the creation of higher
L232: 
L233: nodes in the tree, until the root that contains the whole image.
L234: 
L235: 2.2. Extension to hyperspectral data
L236: 
L237: Constructing an α-tree requires to deﬁne a similarity (or dis-
L238: 
L239: similarity) measure between values of any pair of adjacent
L240: pixels. While such a dissimilarity can be simply written as
L241: 
L242: a difference of grey levels in the panchromatic case, there is
L243: 
L244: no universal solution for multidimensional spaces. Among
L245: 
L246: the most usual choices, we can cite L q norms (with q=
L247: 
L248: 1,2 or even ∞) as well as SAM (Spectral Angle Mapper).
L249: 
L250: However, we have shown in a recent study [2] that these

L315: 3. CONSTRAINED CONNECTIVITY
L316: 
L317: The chaining effect is a well-known issue for the single-
L318: 
L319: linkage paradigm. Since the α-tree is built on this paradigm,
L320: it is naturally affected by this problem. To explain, let us con-
L321: 
L322: sider a series of neighboring pixels with values u 1, . . . , u n. If
L323: 
L324: d(u i, u i+1)≤α for all pairs (i, i+1), these pixels will belong
L325: 
L326: to the same α-CC. This remark holds even for a small value
L327: 
L328: of α, values of neighboring pixels being then always very
L329: 
L330: similar. However, the difference between any pair of pixels
L331: 
L332: within the α-CC (e.g., d(u 1, u n)) might be much larger than
L333: 
L334: α. In this case, pixels with very distinct values are gathered
L335: in a unique α-CC assumed to be of low complexity (low α
L336: 
L337: value). Such a situation is frequently observed on transition
L338: 
L339: regions between objects of different spectral signatures, due
L340: 
L341: to the discretization of edges in digital images [7].

L352: global range of the α-CC i.e., d(p, q)≤ω for all pairs (p, q)
L353: 
L354: of pixel values belonging to this α-CC. Such a criterion leads

L356: to the deﬁnition of the (α, ω)-CCs. Computing this global
L357: 
L358: range is efﬁciently achieved in the grayscale case by storing
L359: 
L360: the minimum and maximum values of each α-CC, and up-
L361:

L364: construction process.

L714: 4. CONCLUSION
L715: 
L716: In this paper we have proposed an active-metric learning
L717: 
L718: method for classification of hyperspectral remote sensing
L719: 
L720: images. While traditional active learning approaches are
L721: 
L722: applied on the original features or on a reduced feature
L723: space obtained by applying feature extraction as a pre-
L724: 
L725: processing step, we have proposed to integrate the two
L726: 
L727: different steps into a unique framework.
L728: 
L729: The experimental results obtained on a real
L730: 
L731: hyperspectral dataset have confirmed the potential validity
L732: 
L733: advantages of the proposed method. Good improvements
L734: 
L735: with respect to a method based on state-of-the-art SVM
L736: 
L737: classification have been demonstrated in terms of
L738: 
L739: classification accuracies and computational time. While the
L740: proposed method is based on LMNN metric learning and a
L741: 
L742: simple selection strategy, more advanced techniques can be
L743: 
L744: investigated to further improve performances.

L390: 3.2. Global range for multivariate data
L391: 
L392: Only very few attempts have been made to address this is-
L393: 
L394: sue. The ﬁrst solution has been proposed by Soille in [3, 8]
L395: 
L396: in the context of remote sensing. A marginal strategy was
L397: suggested, where both α and ω criteria shall be fulﬁlled in all
L398: 
L399: spectral bands to build the (α, ω)-CCs. This presents several
L400: 
L401: drawbacks: i) each band is processed independently of the
L402: 
L403: others, ignoring the possible correlation among bands; ii) the
L404: 
L405: same (local or global) range is imposed on all bands of the
L406: 
L407: image, while the behavior of spectral signatures of different
L408: 
L409: materials might vary very much in the observation spectrum.
L410: 
L411: Conversely, a purely vectorial solution was recently pro-
L412: posed [9]. Assuming a total ordering can be imposed on pixel
L413: 
L414: values, each pixel is described by its rank within the pixel
L415: 
L416: value space. The range of the multivariate set is then deﬁned
L417: 
L418: as the range of the ranks within the set. While this approach
L419: 
L420: exhibits appealing properties, it still requires the deﬁnition of
L421: 
L422: a total ordering. To do so, the standard lexicographical order-
L423: 
L424: ing or one of its variants needs to prioritize the image chan-
L425: 
L426: nels. While this is possible for color images [10], there is no
L427: adequate solution for hyperspectral data yet.
L428: 
L429: 3.3. Efﬁcient overestimation for hyperspectral images
L430: 
L431: Considering the computation of the global range cannot be
L432: 
L433: achieved efﬁciently on multivariate data such as hyperspectral
L434: 
L435: images, we suggest here to rely on an overestimation of it.
L436: 
L437: This approximation is relevant as long as the overestimated
L438: 
L439: global range is still an increasing criterion w.r.t. α.
L440: 
L441: Representing an α-CC by the set of multivariate data it
L442: contains, the simplest scheme to overestimate its global range
L443: 
L444: is to compute the diagonal of the set. To do so, we can approx-
L445: 
L446: imate the set by its bounding box. We only need then to store
L447: 
L448: the minimum and maximum values within each band, which
L449: 
L450: could be very easily updated when merging two α-CCs.
L451: 
L452: However, the overestimation error will increase exponen-
L453: 
L454: tially with the number of dimensions. So we rather rely on the
L455: 
L456: diameter of the bounding sphere. It is known that this tech-
L457: nique leads to much lower estimation error than the bounding
L458: 
L459: box one, when the number of dimensions is high (e.g., in the
L460: 
L461: case of hyperspectral images). Similarly to the case of the
L462: 
L463: bounding box, we can rely on efﬁcient schemes to compute
L464: 
L465: bounding spheres. We only need to store the center of the
L466: 
L467: sphere (i.e., the center of gravity of the set of pixels contained
L468: 
L469: in the α-CC), as well as its radius (i.e., the distance between
L470: 
L471: the center and the furthest element within the α-CC, which
L472: might not correspond to an actual observed pixel). When
L473: 
L474: merging two α-CCs, updating these attributes is trivial: the
L475: 
L476: new center of gravity is a linear combination of the centers
L477: 
L478: of gravity of the two α-CCs to be merged (we also store the
L479: 
L480: α-CCs size); its furthest element is the extreme point at the
L481: 
L482: surface of one of the two spheres from the merging α-CCs.

L581: 6. CONCLUSION
L582: 
L583: Representation of an image through its α-connected com-
L584: 
L585: ponents can lead to a powerful hierarchical model known as
L586: 
L587: α-tree. Furthermore, it can be improved using the constrained
L588: 
L589: connectivity paradigm, leading to (α, ω)-connected compo-
L590: 
L591: nents. These representations allow multiscale image analysis
L592: 
L593: of an image and have been successfully applied in various
L594: 
L595: applications in remote sensing, but mostly for panchromatic
L596: images. Nevertheless, their extension to hyperspectral data
L597: 
L598: is not trivial. The two main stumbling blocks that are to be
L599: 
L600: overcome in such high dimension spaces are i) the deﬁnition
L601: 
L602: of a sensible distance, ii) the design of efﬁcient schemes to
L603: 
L604: support constrained connectivity. While we have addressed
L605: 
L606: the ﬁrst question in a recent study [2], we focus here on
L607: 
L608: the second issue and propose new approximation schemes for
L609: 
L610: computing (α, ω)-connected components and extracting them
L611: from an α-tree. First results are promising but still require
L612: 
L613: a deeper investigation, including a comparison with other
L614: 
L615: spatial-spectral classiﬁcation techniques, as well as using
L616: 
L617: such trees for other challenges raised in remote sensing.
